# Squad Roster Catalog

This file is **canonical** for the Cast Catalog, the External Cast (registered third-party resources, the Verification Gate, and the External Cast Blocklist), and Building a Custom Roster. `.github/instructions/squad/squad-roster.instructions.md` stays canonical for the roster schema, Naming Conventions, `### Dispatchability`, Deliverable Roots, Casting Rules, and Squad Profiles/Squad Packs; read it first for those and for the per-turn resolution rules. Read this file only when casting a role for the first time, recasting after an HVE Core upgrade, applying or registering a pack's external agents, resolving an external role, or assembling a custom roster — ordinary routing resolves an already-seeded role from `team.md` and never needs this file.

## Cast Catalog

The cast catalog is the default casting source and the canonical mapping between squad roles (members) and deployed HVE Core agents, keyed by each agent's exact `name:` frontmatter value. When a project has no `team.md`, the coordinator seeds the roster from this catalog.

The relationship between roles and agents is **many-to-many**. A role names one **Primary** agent — the default the coordinator dispatches — plus optional **Alternate** agents it may resolve to instead when the request matches a **Selection Cue**. A single agent may also fill more than one role (for example, `Codebase Profiler` serves both `researcher` and `security`). See *Relationship Cardinality* below.

Roles that have no stable HVE Core equivalent are marked **thin charter needed**. A thin charter is a small, squad-owned subagent authored under `squad-src/.github/agents/squad/` when the role is actually required; until then the coordinator omits the role or escalates to the user.

Every Primary in this catalog is **dispatchable** (see *Dispatchability* below). Agents that HVE Core ships as user-invocable orchestrators — `PowerPoint Builder`, `Backlog Manager`, `Code Review`, `Documentation`, `RPI Agent`, `Security Reviewer`, `Network ISA-95 Planner`, and the other `disable-model-invocation: true` entry points — are never a Primary and never an Alternate, because `runSubagent` and `task` cannot reach them. Where HVE Core moved a capability from an agent to a skill (research, planning, implementation, review, documentation), the squad dispatches a thin charter that runs that skill.

### External Cast

Some work has no HVE Core capability to wrap and no local charter worth authoring, because a public marketplace already covers the domain. The **external cast** is how the squad reaches such a resource without copying it into this package.

A resource arrives by one of two tiers, and the tier decides almost everything else about it:

* **Bundled** — declared as a pinned dependency in this package's `apm.yml`. A consumer who installs hve-squad alone already has it. There is nothing to install and nothing that can be absent.
* **Opt-in** — recorded here with the command the consumer runs deliberately. Whole verticals are opt-in, because shipping every vertical to every consumer taxes the many to serve the few.

The external cast does not weaken the *Never self-fill an absent role* rule; for an opt-in row it gives that rule an actionable remedy. Only an **opt-in** row has three states:

* **Registered and installed** — behaves exactly like any other catalog role.
* **Registered, not installed** — known and installable, but absent at run time. The coordinator escalates with the install command and stops. The role is never seeded into `team.md` and never appears in a seeded roster as available.
* **Not registered** — outside the cast. The coordinator never fetches, installs, or improvises a resource that has no registry row.

A **bundled** row has two states, not three: present, or a broken installation. It can never be *registered but not installed*, because it ships with the package. A bundled artifact that is genuinely missing is an installation fault to be repaired by reinstalling, not an absent role to escalate to the user.

#### Tier Qualification

A resource is **bundled** only when all five of these hold. Each is a pass-or-fail test, not a judgement call:

1. **It strengthens a role that already exists in the cast catalog.** Decidable from the Role column: if filling the row requires inventing a role, the resource is not bundled.
2. **It is a `skill` or `instruction` kind.** An `agent` or a `plugin` changes who gets dispatched, and that belongs to a deliberate opt-in rather than to everyone by default.
3. **It adds no runtime prerequisite beyond its own bundled files.** No MCP server, no CLI to install, no account, no paid subscription, and no network service requiring credentials. A public unauthenticated API the resource calls on its own is fine.
4. **It stays inside a product or platform the role already works in.** Decidable by naming the product: if using the resource means the role picks up a separate product, tenant, portal, or service it does not otherwise touch, then a vertical is arriving rather than a role being strengthened, and a vertical is opt-in however cleanly it passes the other tests.
5. **It passed the verification gate at a resolved commit SHA**, which is the SHA its `apm.yml` entry pins.

Anything else is **opt-in**. Test 3 does most of the work: the FlowStudio Power Automate skills require a paid MCP subscription, so they are opt-in however useful they are. Test 1 does some of the rest, and it is stricter than it looks — a resource that merely overlaps a role the squad already covers well does not qualify. `microsoft-docs` is the instructive near-miss: it is well authored and genuinely useful, but `researcher` can already fetch `learn.microsoft.com` directly, and the skill expects a Microsoft Learn MCP server to beat that. A resource that needs setup to be marginally better than the capability a role already has is not worth a row in either tier.

**Test 4 exists because tests 1 through 3 alone give the wrong answer for a whole class of resource, and wave 4 is the worked contrast.** `microsoft-agent-framework` and `semantic-kernel` are bundled: they are libraries in .NET and Python, which is what `developer` already writes, so the role picks up no new product. The Power BI skills and `fabric-lakehouse` pass tests 1 through 3 exactly as cleanly — they strengthen `data-scientist`, they are skills, and they need nothing to run — yet they are opt-in, because using them means `data-scientist` takes on Power BI and Fabric, which are separate products with their own tenant, licensing, and workspace. Without test 4 the written rule would ship an entire BI vertical to every consumer by default, which is the outcome the two tiers exist to prevent.

#### External Cast Schema

Registered rows use these columns. Every column is required; a row with a blank cell is not registered. `Prerequisites` takes `none` rather than being left empty.

| Column                   | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                    |
|--------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Role                     | The squad role whose need earned the resource its row; must be a role that exists in the cast catalog above. It records demand, not exclusive access — see the note below this table                                 |
| Tier                     | `bundled` or `opt-in`, assigned by *Tier Qualification* above; the tier decides how the resource arrives, how it is re-verified, and whether it can be absent                |
| Resource                 | The upstream resource identifier exactly as the origin publishes it (for example, `azure-pricing`), because both the pin and the install command depend on it being exact    |
| Resource Kind            | `agent`, `skill`, `instruction`, or `plugin`; the kind determines how the resource resolves (see *Resolving an External Role*)                                               |
| Origin                   | The publishing repository and the path to the resource within it, so the row can be re-verified without a search                                                            |
| Install or Entry         | For `bundled`, the pinned `apm.yml` dependency entry including its `#sha`. For `opt-in`, the exact command the consumer runs, copied from the origin's own documentation      |
| License                  | The license the resource is published under, recorded so the attribution posture in `.github/instructions/licensing-posture.instructions.md` can be applied                  |
| Prerequisites            | Any MCP server, CLI, account, or subscription the resource needs before it works, or `none`; a `bundled` row is always `none`, because test 3 of *Tier Qualification* says so |
| Dispatchability Verified | `yes`, `no`, or `n/a` with the reason; `n/a` is correct for a skill or instruction, which is reached rather than dispatched (see *Reaching an External Resource*)               |
| Verified On              | The ISO date the verification gate last passed for this row; this is the column the re-verification policy reads                                                             |

`Resource Kind` carries most of the weight, because kinds resolve differently:

* An **agent** may become a role's Primary or Alternate once installed, provided it passed the gate. An agent is always opt-in.
* A **skill** or **instruction** is never a Primary. It extends the capability of a role that already exists, and it is reached rather than dispatched.
* A **plugin** is a bundle. Register the specific agent or skill inside it that the role needs, and name the plugin only in the install command; do not register a bundle as though it were a single resource.

**The `Role` column records which role's need earned the row, not who is allowed to use the resource.** For a `skill` or `instruction` the distinction matters, because *Reaching an External Resource* below puts an installed skill in the runtime's skills tree where every agent in the session can see it. A second role reaching the same skill is therefore normal, not a duplicate registration, and it does not trigger the gate's collision check — which asks whether two resources claim the same job, not whether two roles read the same reference. Register one row against the role that most directly needs the resource, and add a second row only when a different role needs it for a *different* job that the first row's row would misdescribe. Where two roles share a skill, say where the line between them falls in both of their Selection Cues; `release-engineer` and `supply-chain` sharing `github-actions-hardening` is the worked case.

Four bundled rows, deliberately few. `azure-pricing` strengthens `cost-manager`, whose Primary already performs Azure pricing lookups, and it calls a public unauthenticated API; the `Squad Cost Manager` charter names it explicitly in its Step 2, which is the *explicit reach* path described below. `gdpr-compliant` gives `privacy` the code-level engineering rules — data models, retention jobs, logging, pseudonymization — that sit underneath the DPIA and data-map work its Primary already does. `microsoft-agent-framework` and `semantic-kernel` give `developer` the AI application build side that HVE Core covers nowhere, and they are libraries in the languages the squad already writes rather than a separate product. All four were gated against `9db369d00f121542e1c99fd9b6cd6f707bade765`, the same commit their `apm.yml` entries pin, so the recorded outcome stays checkable after upstream moves on.

**The bundled test that decides most of this set is test 3, and the wave 4 harvest is what proved it.** The E-007 list of resources that strengthen existing roles turned out to be almost entirely operational Azure and GitHub skills: `az-cost-optimize` names two authenticated MCP servers in its own prerequisites, `azure-deployment-preflight` and `import-infrastructure-as-code` need an authenticated Azure CLI and a live subscription, and `codeql`, `secret-scanning`, and `dependabot` author their configuration for free but need GitHub security entitlements to operate. Each is genuinely useful and each is opt-in, which is the tier working as designed rather than a shortfall.

The opt-in rows arrived with the vertical packs, with that harvest, and with the two delivery-discipline roles below. A resource earns a row only when a role actually needs it; none is registered to demonstrate a tier. Every path shape — agent file, skill directory, and plugin directory — was confirmed resolvable against `github/awesome-copilot` before any row was written.

**Two verticals are registered against widened existing roles rather than against a pack**, because no upstream agent in either survived the gate. The Power BI and Fabric skills strengthen `data-scientist`, which already owns data profiling and analytical deliverables and now reaches semantic-model review, DAX optimization, report design, and Lakehouse fundamentals as well. The AI application engineering skills strengthen `developer`, which already owns building the application. Inventing a `bi-analyst` or `ai-engineer` role would have put two roles on one job, which the casting rules call worse than a missing role.

**Reaching a widened role is not the same as reaching a pack, and it is worth saying how.** A pack is applied; a widened role is simply on the roster or it is not. `developer` is part of the methodology spine, so the AI application engineering skills are reachable from every profile without anything being added. `data-scientist` is narrower: it is seeded by `full` and `product` only. In any other profile a Power BI, DAX, semantic-model, Fabric, or Lakehouse request matches the `data-scientist` routing row, finds the role absent, and the coordinator offers to add it — the same offer it makes for an opt-in role — rather than declining or answering from a role that does not own the work. That path works, but it is discovered at the moment of need rather than at build time, which is the honest cost of registering a vertical against a role instead of shipping it as a pack.

**Fabric coverage is thin and is recorded as thin.** `fabric-lakehouse` is a Lakehouse primer: OneLake, Delta tables, schemas and shortcuts, SQL analytics endpoint, materialized and Spark views, OneLake security, and V-Order and `OPTIMIZE` tuning. It does not cover Data Factory pipelines, Warehouse architecture, Real-Time Intelligence, deployment pipelines, semantic-model ALM, or capacity administration. A request in those areas has no registered resource behind it and is escalated rather than answered from the primer.

**The two delivery-discipline roles are external for the same reason the verticals are.** QA automation and release engineering are the last uncovered gaps that upstream actually fills: HVE Core ships test-*authoring conventions* (`pester`, `python-tests`, `csharp-tests`, `rust-tests`) with nothing that writes or runs a test, and it ships `workflows.instructions.md`, `ci-owned-validation.instructions.md`, and the `gh-code-scanning` skill with nothing that authors a pipeline. Both therefore rest on a registered opt-in agent rather than on a squad charter, because a charter with no skill beneath it would invent the capability rather than expose one — the same reasoning that keeps `devrel` unselectable.

**One registered row is bundled-eligible and is deliberately left opt-in, and the case for it is argued against a role other than the one that registered it.** `github-actions-hardening` sits under `release-engineer`, because that is the role that most directly needs it: it changes the workflow files the skill audits. The bundled case is argued against `supply-chain`, which reaches the same skill ambiently for posture evidence, and the reason is the tier's own logic rather than an inconsistency. A bundled resource ships to every consumer, so it is only worth bundling if the role it strengthens is one most consumers carry — and `supply-chain` is seeded by `full`, `security`, and `compliance`, while `release-engineer` is seeded by no profile at all. Assessed against `supply-chain` the skill passes all five *Tier Qualification* tests: it strengthens a role that already exists, it is a skill, it needs nothing at run time, GitHub Actions is a platform this repository already lives on, and it gated clean. It stays opt-in only because promoting it means adding an `apm.yml` pin and a curated entry to `scripts/Update-ApmDependencies.ps1`, which is a dependency-manifest change rather than a catalog change. The qualification is recorded here so the promotion is a decision someone makes rather than a discovery someone repeats.

**AWS is a pack and there is no `gcp` anything.** The `aws` pack rests on three verified agents that split cleanly by shape — landing zone and multi-account, hands-on service work, and serverless — plus a fourth for incident triage, so it produces two roles rather than four. The multi-cloud material upstream is AWS-only. The `terraform-aws-*` skills named in the original coverage survey were probed at two paths, `skills/terraform-aws-iam/SKILL.md` and `skills/terraform-aws-vpc/SKILL.md`, and both return 404 at the pinned commit; that establishes those two paths are absent rather than that no such skill exists, so the family was dropped from the candidate set as unresolvable rather than recorded as proven absent. Registering a path that returns 404 would give a consumer an install command that fails. See *Registered Packs* for why AWS is a pack while `azure` remains a profile.

#### Verification Gate

Run these checks in order before a resource is registered. The gate is deliberately cheap so that re-running it is never the reason a row goes stale.

1. **Read the resource's frontmatter at the origin.** Do not register from a listing, a description, or a search result; the frontmatter is the only authority for the checks below.
2. **Check `disable-model-invocation`.** A resource that sets it to `true` can never be a Primary or an Alternate, because `runSubagent` and `task` cannot reach it. This is the same rule *Dispatchability* applies to local agents.
3. **Check the declared `tools:` list against locally available tools.** An agent that requests tools this project does not have degrades silently rather than failing loudly, which is worse than being absent.
4. **Check for a delegated-worker input contract.** A resource that validates a required parent artifact, lane, or cycle before acting is a worker, not a role; *Worker Agents Are Not Roles* applies unchanged.
5. **Check for a collision with a capability the roster can already reach.** Two cases fail this check, not one: a capability HVE Core already deploys, and a resource already registered against the same role for the same job. A duplicate is worse than a gap either way, because the roster stops being a single source of truth about who owns the work.
6. **Check that a role actually needs it.** A resource earns a row only when an existing role's work calls for it. Quality is not the test; demand is. Register nothing to demonstrate a tier, to fill out a domain, or because it may be useful later.
7. **Check the resource's own documentation for a runtime prerequisite.** Frontmatter and the `tools:` list do not surface these: `microsoft-docs` states its Microsoft Learn MCP dependency only in prose, and the FlowStudio skills state a paid subscription only in prose. Record whatever it needs, because this check decides the tier and fills the `Prerequisites` column.
8. **Record the licence and the origin path**, so attribution and re-verification are both possible from the row alone.

Record the outcome in one of exactly two places, never neither:

* **Accepted** — add the row to *Registered External Cast* with `Verified On` set to the date the gate ran.
* **Rejected** — add the resource to the *External Cast Blocklist* with the failing check as the reason, so the next maintainer does not re-evaluate it from scratch.

Add an entry whenever a candidate fails the gate. Two standing rules govern the common cases. **A resource that duplicates a capability the roster can already reach is blocked regardless of its quality**, whether that capability is one HVE Core deploys or one already registered against the same role, because the cost of an ambiguous owner exceeds the benefit of a second implementation. **A resource no role needs is blocked even when it passes every other check**, because a registry that collects what might be useful stops being a statement of what the squad can actually do. Removing a blocklist entry requires the collision, the absent demand, or the gate failure to have actually gone away, recorded with a fresh date.

#### Resolving an External Role

External resolution extends *Resolving a Role to an Agent* rather than replacing it:

1. **Skill and instruction kinds never resolve directly.** The role resolves to its local Primary as usual, and the resource extends what that role can do. See *Reaching an External Resource* below for how it gets used.
2. **Agent kinds resolve through the normal sequence** once installed, and are subject to every casting rule that applies to a local agent, including one Primary per role. Every agent row is opt-in.
3. **A registered opt-in agent that is not installed is an absent role.** The coordinator stops and escalates, and must not perform the work itself or substitute a non-mapped agent. This is the same stop, not a softer variant.
4. **The escalation names the remedy.** State the role, the registered resource, the exact `Install or Entry` command from its row, its `Prerequisites`, and the origin and license, so the user can act immediately and knowingly. Offer the choice the roster already offers for any absent role: install it, name a substitute, or remove the role.
5. **A registered but uninstalled opt-in role is never seeded.** The Scribe writes it into `team.md` only after the resource is present, so a roster never advertises capability the project does not have.
6. **A missing bundled artifact is an installation fault, not an absent role.** It ships with the package, so the remedy is reinstalling hve-squad rather than asking the user to fetch anything. Report it as a broken installation and name the entry from the row.

#### Reaching an External Resource

A skill or instruction is never dispatched, so "how does the role reach it" is a separate question from "how does the role resolve". Once present, an external skill sits in the agent runtime's skills tree where every agent in a session can see it, and it reaches its role by one of two paths. The difference in guarantee is real, and the roster states which path applies rather than implying they are the same:

* **Explicit reach, for a role whose Primary is a squad-owned charter** under `squad-src/.github/agents/squad/`. The charter names the skill in its own instructions, so the reach is deterministic and reviewable. This is the stronger guarantee and the one to prefer whenever the charter is ours to edit. Every role whose Primary is a `Squad`-prefixed charter is in this group, and every such role that currently has a registered resource is wired for it: `cost-manager`, `developer`, `deployer`, `iac-author`, `azure-architect`, and `data-scientist` (the Power BI and Fabric skills, named explicitly in `squad-data-scientist.agent.md`). `performance`, `observability`, `vuln-manager`, and `risk-manager` are in the group too and simply have no registered resource yet. Being in this group is a claim about the charter, so when a resource is registered against one of these roles, wire the charter in the same change rather than leaving the claim ahead of the wiring.
* **Ambient reach, for a role whose Primary is a deployed HVE Core agent.** Those agent files are produced by `apm install` and are never hand-edited, so the skill cannot be named in them. The agent finds the skill through ordinary skill discovery, which is triggered by the skill's own description rather than by a roster rule. This is a weaker, non-deterministic guarantee. `security`, `privacy`, `supply-chain`, and `architect` are in this group.
* **Ambient reach is also the only option for a role whose Primary is an external agent.** A registered opt-in agent installed from a marketplace is no more editable here than a deployed HVE Core agent is, so a skill registered against that role cannot be named in its Primary either. `pp-architect`, `pp-connector`, `m365-agent-architect`, `m365-agent-integrator`, `qa-engineer`, `release-engineer`, `aws-architect`, and `aws-diagnose` are the current cases, and every Power Platform, Microsoft 365, QA, release-engineering, and AWS skill registered against them reaches its role this way. The remedy when that is not good enough is the same one the closing paragraph gives: author a squad charter that owns the work and names the skill, and cast the external agent as an Alternate behind it.

Both paths apply to both tiers, and the tier decides only whether the resource is present to begin with. A **bundled** skill ships with the package, so its reach path is live as soon as the package is installed. An **opt-in** skill reaches its role the same two ways, but only after the consumer runs its install command; before that it is simply absent, and a role that depends on it is weaker rather than broken. When an opt-in skill is worth wiring explicitly, wire the charter for it as though it were bundled — the charter should say what it does when the skill is not present.

Do not paper over the difference between the two paths. When a resource matters enough that ambient reach is not good enough, the honest options are to author a squad charter for that role or to leave the work with the role's existing Primary.

#### Re-Verification Policy

A registered row points at a repository that changes daily, so a single verification at registration time is not enough. What replaces it depends on the tier, because a pin removes the moving target and an install command does not.

**Bundled rows re-verify when their pin moves.** A pinned commit SHA is immutable, so the row cannot decay while the pin holds and a calendar trigger would be ceremony. The risk arrives at the moment someone advances the pin, which is the same risk `Get-HveCoreCastDelta.ps1` already guards for the hve-core dependency: a moved SHA can silently break a roster row. Re-run the gate at the new SHA before the moved pin is committed.

**Opt-in rows re-verify on triggers**, because nothing pins them. Re-run the gate for an affected row when any of these happen:

* A dispatch against a registered external agent fails or returns nothing. Treat this exactly as the roster already treats a broken dispatch: the runtime guard escalates, and the registry row is the thing to correct.
* A squad build or roster seed selects a profile that carries an external role. The build is the natural checkpoint, because it is the moment the row is about to matter.
* `Verified On` is more than 90 days old at the time of a build. This is the backstop for rows that no other trigger has touched.

One trigger applies to **both** tiers: when the HVE Core dependency is upgraded, re-check every registered row for collision. Upstream consolidation can turn a registered external resource into a duplicate of a newly deployed capability, and a duplicate belongs on the blocklist regardless of how it arrives.

The same upgrade trigger reaches past the external cast. A charter binds to upstream capability in three ways — a dispatchable agent name, a named skill, and a deployed prompt path — and all three break the same silent way when upstream renames or removes one. `scripts/Get-HveCoreCastDelta.ps1` compares all three surfaces between two hve-core refs and marks the delta breaking when the squad still references something the new ref no longer exposes, which is what stops an automated pin bump from releasing a squad whose charters resolve to nothing.

Re-verification ends in one of three states: the row passes unchanged and `Verified On` advances; the row still resolves but its entry, prerequisites, or license changed, so those cells are corrected and `Verified On` advances; or the resource fails a check and the row moves to the blocklist with the failing reason. A row is never left with a stale `Verified On` and an unchanged date.

### Building a Custom Roster

When no named profile fits — or when one is close but not exact — the coordinator helps the user assemble a custom roster rather than inventing one. The coordinator presents the role menu below — each row is a role the squad can dispatch, the plain-language work it contributes, and the deployed agent that fills it by default — and the user picks any subset. The user may start from a profile's roles and add or remove from there; when they do, the roster is recorded as a custom roster derived from that profile, because any change to a profile's exact member set makes it custom.

Three rules bound a custom roster so it never references work the squad cannot actually do:

* **`scribe` is always included** — it owns ordinary squad-state writes after Cost Preflight and is never offered as optional.
* **The methodology spine (`researcher`, `lead`, `developer`, `tester`) is recommended** so the Research → Plan → Implement → Review cycle stays intact. The user may drop a spine role, but that disables the matching leg and the Implementation Gate in `squad-routing.instructions.md` escalates if it is later needed.
* **Only catalog roles with a dispatchable Primary are selectable.** The coordinator never invents a role or an agent outside the cast catalog. A role whose mapped agent is not installed or is not dispatchable, or a role with no backing capability at all — `devrel`, `networking`, `gcp`, and `identity` — is flagged and left out rather than seeded. A role backed by a registered **opt-in** *External Cast* resource that is not installed is offered with its install command rather than seeded, and becomes selectable once the resource is present. A **bundled** resource never creates this situation, because it ships with the package.

When the roles a user is reaching for are already a registered **pack**, offer the pack by name instead of walking them through the menu row by row. Applying a pack keeps the roster's provenance recorded as a profile plus that pack, where a hand-picked equivalent would be recorded only as `custom`.

The menu mirrors the Cast Catalog above; each item names the role, the deployed agent that fills it by default (in parentheses), and the user-facing gloss.

* **researcher** (Squad Researcher) — Investigates the codebase, the web, and connected tools to gather the context the squad needs.
* **lead** (Squad Lead) — Plans the work: breaks a request into phases, sequences them, and names the deliverables and their owners.
* **developer** (Squad Implementor) — Implements the change: writes and edits code to carry out the plan.
* **tester** (Squad Reviewer) — Reviews changes for quality, correctness, and standards before they ship.
* **qa-engineer** (QA) — Writes and runs the tests: plans what to cover, hunts edge cases and hostile inputs, and reports defects you can reproduce. Where `tester` reads a change, this role tests it. Opt-in: rests on a registered external agent you install.
* **challenger** (Squad Challenger) — Plays devil's advocate: pressure-tests plans and assumptions, and checks that a plan is backed by the research it claims to rest on.
* **architect** (System Architecture Reviewer) — Reviews system-design tradeoffs and well-architected alignment; can produce ADRs.
* **security** (Security Planner) — Plans security: threat-models the work, identifies risks, and maps controls.
* **supply-chain** (SSSC Planner) — Assesses how the software is built, signed, and released: OpenSSF Scorecard, SLSA, Sigstore, and SBOM posture, and the backlog to improve it.
* **vuln-manager** (Squad Vulnerability Manager) — Works out whether a published vulnerability actually reaches your product, and drafts the VEX statement that records the answer for a human to merge.
* **rai** (RAI Planner) — Assesses responsible-AI concerns such as fairness, harm, and transparency for AI/ML work.
* **privacy** (Privacy Planner) — Maps personal-data flows, tests DPIA thresholds, and plans privacy controls.
* **accessibility** (Accessibility Framework Assessor) — Assesses the product against WCAG 2.2, ARIA, Section 508, and EN 301 549, and discovers the runtime surfaces and interaction states that need assessing.
* **fact-checker** (Finding Deep Verifier) — Independently verifies findings and claims before the squad trusts them.
* **risk-manager** (Squad Risk Manager) — Keeps the project risk register: what could go wrong, how likely and how bad, who owns it, and what the mitigation is.
* **performance** (Squad Performance Planner) — Turns "it should be fast" into measurable objectives, error budgets, and a load-test plan; plans the tests but never runs them.
* **observability** (Squad Observability Planner) — Designs what the system emits and what it is called: traces, metrics, logs, and how personal data is kept out of them.
* **designer** (UX UI Designer) — Researches users and designs the experience: journey maps, jobs-to-be-done, and accessibility.
* **product-owner** (Functional Planner) — Turns a PRD into a validated work-item hierarchy for Azure DevOps, GitHub, or Jira. Plans the work items; `backlog-executor` writes them.
* **backlog-executor** (Squad Backlog Executor) — Creates the planned work items in your live Azure DevOps, GitHub, or Jira project, after showing you exactly what it will write and waiting for your approval. Opt-in: no profile includes it, and the squad offers to add it the first time you ask for a tracker write.
* **analyst** (PRD Builder) — Captures product and business requirements as a PRD or BRD.
* **data-scientist** (Squad Data Scientist) — Profiles data, builds exploratory-analysis notebooks and dashboards, authors dataops pipelines and feasibility studies, and sets up ML experimentation.
* **prompt-engineer** (Squad Prompt Engineer) — Authors, refactors, and analyses prompt artifacts (prompts, instructions, agents, and skills) and designs AI evaluation datasets.
* **technical-writer** (Squad Technical Writer) — Authors and maintains documentation that stays in step with the code.
* **presenter** (PowerPoint Subagent) — Builds slide decks and executive summaries through the PowerPoint skill pipeline.
* **experimenter** (Experiment Designer) — Designs a Minimum Viable Experiment to validate the riskiest assumption.
* **cost-manager** (Squad Cost Manager) — Estimates Azure cost and applies FinOps and Well-Architected cost guidance.
* **azure-architect** (Squad Azure Architect) — Authors Azure high- and low-level designs with AVM modules and landing-zone patterns.
* **iac-author** (Squad IaC Author) — Converts an Azure design into Bicep or Terraform; authors IaC but never deploys.
* **deployer** (Squad Deployer) — Runs Azure deployments behind a human approval gate; defaults to a read-only dry run.
* **release-engineer** (GitHub Actions Expert) — Builds and hardens the delivery pipeline: GitHub Actions workflows, pinned actions, OIDC instead of stored secrets, CI cost and duration, environments and approvals, and the rollout and rollback plan. Builds the pipeline; never runs a deployment itself. Opt-in: rests on a registered external agent you install.
* **aws-architect** (aws-principal-architect) — Designs AWS workloads: which services, how the accounts and landing zone are laid out, and the CDK, SAM, or CloudFormation to build it, judged against the AWS Well-Architected pillars. Part of the `aws` pack, so it arrives only when that pack is installed and applied.
* **aws-diagnose** (AWS Incident Triage) — Works an AWS incident read-only from the alarm to an evidence-backed root-cause hypothesis, using CloudWatch metrics, logs, and traces; recommends a mitigation but never applies one. Part of the `aws` pack.
* **modernizer** (Squad Modernization Planner) — Plans framework, dependency, and cloud-migration modernization; SQL migration recommendation and prerequisite/readiness cues resolve to Squad SQL Migration Advisor.
* **asbuilt-author** (Squad As-Built Author) — Documents already-deployed infrastructure (inventory, compliance, runbook, DR); strictly read-only.
* **azure-diagnose** (Squad Azure Diagnose) — Triages deployed Azure resources read-only into ranked hypotheses and leads the incident through to its root-cause record; recommends but never applies fixes.
* **pp-architect** (Power Platform Expert) — Designs the Power Platform solution: which of Power Apps, Power Automate, Power Pages, Dataverse, and Copilot Studio to use, how environments and DLP policies are set up, and how the data model and solution lifecycle hang together. Part of the `power-platform` pack, so it arrives only when that pack is installed and applied.
* **pp-connector** (Power Platform MCP Integration Expert) — Builds Power Platform custom connectors and wires them into Copilot Studio agents; writes the connector files and prepares them for certification, but never publishes one to your tenant. Part of the `power-platform` pack.
* **m365-agent-architect** (Declarative Agents Architect) — Designs a Microsoft 365 Copilot declarative agent: what it should be able to do, how its instructions and conversation starters read, and whether it is defined as a JSON manifest or in TypeSpec. Writes the definition and the design notes; never provisions the agent in your tenant. Part of the `m365-copilot` pack, so it arrives only when that pack is installed and applied.
* **m365-agent-integrator** (MCP M365 Agent Expert) — Connects a Microsoft 365 Copilot agent to the systems behind it: MCP server tools, sign-in through Entra, and Microsoft Graph. Plans the tenant rollout and stops at the handoff rather than deploying it for you. Part of the `m365-copilot` pack.
* **intake-validator** (PRD Quality Reviewer) — Validates that requirement and input artifacts are complete and clear before the squad builds on them. Seeded in the `product` and `full` profiles; addable to any roster; dispatched only by the conditional intake gate.
* **scribe** (Squad Scribe) — Writes squad state: decisions, history, and memory. Always included; never optional.
